content:
Unit 1 Overview & Syllabus Breakdown

Computer Systems and Organisation (Unit 1) forms the foundational building block of CBSE Class 11 Computer Science (Subject Code 083), carrying a weightage of 10 Marks in the theory examination.

This master module provides an original, in-depth breakdown of the entire Unit 1 syllabus. Studying this unit equips students with a clear understanding of how electronic hardware components interact with system software, execute binary instructions, perform digital logic operations, convert data across number systems, and represent human language using universal encoding schemes.

Syllabus Blueprint & Key Topics

  • Basic Computer Organisation: Computer architecture, hardware, software, CPU (ALU, CU, Registers), Memory hierarchy (Primary, Cache, Secondary), Units of Memory.
  • Types of Software: System software (OS, Utilities, Device Drivers), Programming tools & translators (Assembler, Compiler, Interpreter), Application software (General & Customized).
  • Operating System (OS): Core functions of OS (Process, Memory, File, Device, Security), OS user interfaces (CLI vs GUI vs NUI).
  • Boolean Logic: Truth values, logic gates (NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR), truth tables, De Morgan’s Laws & proofs, logic circuits.
  • Number Systems: Decimal, Binary, Octal, Hexadecimal number systems and conversion algorithms with worked examples.
  • Encoding Schemes: Character representation using ASCII, ISCII, and Unicode (UTF-8, UTF-32).

1. Introduction to Computer Architecture

A computer is an electronic, programmable data-processing device that accepts raw data as Input, processes it according to stored instructions in the Central Processing Unit (CPU), stores data in Memory, and generates meaningful Output.

The standard model governing modern computers is the Von Neumann Architecture, proposed by mathematician John von Neumann in 1945. It introduces the concept of a Stored-Program Computer, where both program instructions and data reside in a shared memory system.

Functional Components of a Computer System

  1. Input Unit: Captures signals or keystrokes from the physical environment and converts human-readable data into machine-understandable binary signals (0s and 1s).
  2. Central Processing Unit (CPU): Often termed the brain of the computer. It executes instructions, performs numerical calculations, evaluates logical conditions, and coordinates signal flow across all peripherals.
  3. Storage/Memory Unit: Retains data, program code, and intermediate computation results temporarily (Primary Memory) or permanently (Secondary Memory).
  4. Output Unit: Converts binary results produced by the CPU into human-understandable visual, auditory, or physical formats.
  5. System Bus: High-speed parallel electrical wires that connect the CPU, memory, and I/O devices. It comprises the Data Bus (bidirectional, carries data), Address Bus (unidirectional, carries memory addresses), and Control Bus (carries control signals like read/write commands).

2. Study Roadmap for Unit 1

To master Unit 1 effectively for school assessments and CBSE board preparations, navigate through each specialized topic module sequentially:

  1. Basic Computer Organisation: Understand CPU registers, memory types, and memory units.
  2. Types of Software: Learn the crucial differences between compilers and interpreters.
  3. Operating System: Master OS resource management functions and CLI/GUI differences.
  4. Boolean Logic: Practice truth tables, gate symbols, and De Morgan’s law proofs.
  5. Number Systems: Practice step-by-step conversions between Binary, Octal, Decimal, and Hexadecimal.
  6. Encoding Schemes: Memorize ASCII ranges and understand Unicode UTF-8 benefits.

Revision Questions & Answers

Q1: What is the Von Neumann Architecture?
Ans: It is a computer design model where CPU executes stored program instructions and data fetched from a shared memory unit using a system bus.

Q2: What are the three components of the System Bus?
Ans: 1. Data Bus (carries actual data), 2. Address Bus (carries target memory/device addresses), 3. Control Bus (transmits timing and command signals).

1. Hardware and Software Overview

A computer system functions through a seamless synthesis of physical components (Hardware) and intangible instruction sets (Software).

  • Hardware: The physical, tangible electrical and mechanical components of a computer system (e.g., CPU chip, RAM modules, motherboard, hard drive, keyboard, monitor).
  • Software: A set of programs, procedures, and algorithms written in a programming language that instructs hardware to perform specific tasks.

2. Input and Output Devices

Peripherals connect the internal processing unit of a computer to the external world.

Key Input Devices

  • Keyboard & Mouse: Standard text input and pointing devices.
  • Scanner: Captures printed documents or photographs and converts them into digital raster images. Types include Flatbed and Handheld scanners.
  • Optical Character Reader (OCR): Analyzes scanned document images and converts printed text into editable text strings.
  • Optical Mark Reader (OMR): Detects presence or absence of pencil/ink marks on standardized objective answer sheets.
  • Magnetic Ink Character Recognition (MICR): Reads special magnetic ink characters printed on bank cheques (used extensively in banking for fast cheque clearing).
  • Barcode Reader / QR Code Scanner: Reads pattern of parallel lines or 2D matrix blocks to fetch product or URL metadata.
  • Microphone & Webcam: Capture analog audio waveforms and video frames, digitizing them for processing or transmission.

Key Output Devices

  • Monitors: Visual display units. Modern displays use LCD (Liquid Crystal Display), LED (Light Emitting Diode), or OLED technology. Display quality is determined by resolution (pixels) and refresh rate (Hz).
  • Printers: Produce hard-copy output on paper.
    • Impact Printers: Physical contact between print head and paper (e.g., Dot Matrix Printer). Loud, slower, but low cost per page.
    • Non-Impact Printers: Spray ink or fuse toner powder onto paper without physical impact (e.g., Inkjet Printers, Laser Printers). Quiet, high speed, high resolution.
  • Speakers & Headphones: Convert digital audio signals into audible sound waves via digital-to-analog converters (DAC).
  • Plotters: Specialized vector output devices that draw continuous high-precision lines on large paper sheets (used for architectural blueprints and engineering diagrams).
  • Digital Projectors: Project computer display output onto large screens using Light Processing (DLP/LCD) technology.

3. Central Processing Unit (CPU)

The Central Processing Unit (CPU) executes machine code instructions during the Fetch-Decode-Execute cycle. It consists of three core sub-components:

Internal Components of CPU

  1. Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): Performs mathematical operations (Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication, Division) and logical comparisons (AND, OR, NOT, Less Than, Greater Than, Equal To).
  2. Control Unit (CU): The central supervisor. It fetches instructions from main memory, decodes what operation needs to be performed, and issues electronic control signals to ALU, registers, and memory to execute it.
  3. CPU Registers: Ultra-fast, temporary storage cells located directly inside the CPU package. They hold data currently being processed.
    • Accumulator (AC): Stores intermediate results generated by the ALU.
    • Program Counter (PC): Holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched and executed.
    • Memory Address Register (MAR): Holds the memory location address currently being read from or written to.
    • Memory Data Register (MDR) / Memory Buffer Register (MBR): Holds the actual data fetched from or ready to be sent to RAM.
    • Instruction Register (IR): Holds the current instruction fetched from memory while it is being decoded by the CU.

4. Computer Memory Hierarchy

Memory in a computer system is organized in a multi-tier hierarchy balancing speed, capacity, and cost per bit.

Speed & Cost per Bit (Highest to Lowest): CPU Registers > Cache Memory > Primary Memory (RAM/ROM) > Secondary Storage (SSD/HDD).

Storage Capacity (Lowest to Highest): CPU Registers < Cache Memory < Primary Memory < Secondary Storage.

Primary Memory (Main Memory)

Primary memory is directly accessible by the CPU via the system bus.

  • RAM (Random Access Memory): Volatile memory (loses all stored contents when power is switched off). Read/Write memory used to store active programs and operating system files currently in execution.
    • SRAM (Static RAM): Made of transistor flip-flops. Very fast, expensive, does not require periodic electrical refresh. Used in CPU cache.
    • DRAM (Dynamic RAM): Made of tiny capacitors and transistors. Must be refreshed electrically thousands of times per second. Slower than SRAM, cheaper, used for system RAM.
  • ROM (Read Only Memory): Non-volatile memory (retains contents even when power is turned off). Holds permanent system bootstrap loader programs (BIOS/UEFI) required to turn on the computer.
    • PROM (Programmable ROM): Written once by manufacturer or user using special equipment. Cannot be erased.
    • EPROM (Erasable Programmable ROM): Contents can be erased by exposing the chip to strong Ultraviolet (UV) light for 20-30 minutes.
    • EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable ROM): Contents can be erased and rewritten electrically byte-by-byte (used in modern flash BIOS).

Cache Memory

Cache memory is a small, extremely fast SRAM buffer situated between the CPU cores and main RAM. It stores frequently accessed data and instructions to eliminate CPU wait-states caused by slower RAM access speeds.

  • L1 Cache: Built directly inside each CPU core (Fastest, smallest size e.g., 32KB to 128KB).
  • L2 Cache: Dedicated per-core or shared cache (e.g., 512KB to 2MB).
  • L3 Cache: Shared across all CPU cores on the chip (e.g., 8MB to 64MB+).

Secondary Storage (Auxiliary Memory)

Secondary memory is non-volatile, high-capacity, inexpensive storage used for permanent data retention (operating systems, application software, media, user files).

  • Hard Disk Drive (HDD): Uses spinning magnetic platters and read/write heads. Mechanical, susceptible to shock damage, lower speed (100-200 MB/s).
  • Solid State Drive (SSD): Uses non-volatile NAND flash memory chips. No moving parts, highly durable, extremely fast read/write speeds (500 MB/s to 7000+ MB/s NVMe).
  • Optical Disks: Use laser beams to read/write pits and lands on reflective disk surfaces. Includes CD-ROM (700 MB capacity), DVD (4.7 GB single layer), and Blu-ray Disks (25 GB to 50 GB).
  • Flash Drives / SD Cards: Portable EEPROM flash storage devices using USB or memory card interfaces.

5. Units of Memory Measurement

Digital computers represent data in binary digits (bits). Memory capacity is measured using standardized binary power metrics ($2^{10} = 1024$).

Unit Name Abbreviation Equivalent Value Power of 2 Equivalent
Binary Digitbit0 or 1$2^0$ bit
Nibble-4 bits-
ByteB8 bits$2^3$ bits
KilobyteKB1024 Bytes$2^{10}$ Bytes
MegabyteMB1024 KB$2^{20}$ Bytes
GigabyteGB1024 MB$2^{30}$ Bytes
TerabyteTB1024 GB$2^{40}$ Bytes
PetabytePB1024 TB$2^{50}$ Bytes

Revision Questions & Answers

Q1: Differentiate between RAM and ROM.
Ans: RAM is volatile read/write memory storing active runtime data. ROM is non-volatile read-only memory storing permanent system startup code (BIOS).

Q2: What is the purpose of Program Counter (PC) register in CPU?
Ans: The Program Counter register holds the memory address of the next instruction waiting to be fetched and executed by the Control Unit.

Q3: Convert 4 MB into Bytes.
Ans: $4 \text{ MB} = 4 \times 1024 \text{ KB} = 4 \times 1024 \times 1024 \text{ Bytes} = 4,194,304 \text{ Bytes} = 4 \times 2^{20} \text{ Bytes}$.

subject: CS
title: Types of Software, Utilities & Translators
description: Original study guide on Types of Software for Class 11 CS. Features system software, system utilities, device drivers, application software, and language translators (Assembler, Compiler, Interpreter comparison).
content:
1. What is Software?

Software is a collection of programs, data, and documentation that tells computer hardware what tasks to perform and how to carry them out. Software bridges the gap between human intentions and electronic transistor circuits.

Software is classified into three major categories:

  1. System Software
  2. Programming Tools & Translators
  3. Application Software

2. System Software

System software includes programs that directly control hardware operations, manage system resources, and provide a stable execution platform for application software.

A. Operating System (OS)

The Operating System is the primary system software that manages hardware components (CPU, memory, storage, devices) and provides a user interface. Examples: Microsoft Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS.

B. System Utilities

System utilities are specialized maintenance tools designed to support, optimize, configure, and protect the computer system.

  • Antivirus Software: Scans system files and memory to detect, quarantine, and remove malware, viruses, spyware, and ransomware (e.g., Windows Defender, Norton, Kaspersky).
  • Disk Defragmenter: Reorganizes fragmented files stored on magnetic hard drives into contiguous disk sectors to improve file read/write access speed.
  • Disk Cleanup Utility: Identifies and deletes unnecessary temporary files, cache, and system logs to free up storage space.
  • Backup & Recovery Tools: Creates duplicate copies of important data onto external drives or cloud storage to prevent data loss in case of hardware failure.
  • File Compression Utilities: Reduces file size using lossless compression algorithms for efficient storage and fast transmission (e.g., WinRAR, 7-Zip, gzip).

C. Device Drivers

A device driver is a specialized software program that acts as a translator between the Operating System and a specific hardware peripheral (e.g., graphics card driver, printer driver, Wi-Fi adapter driver).

Without a device driver, the OS cannot communicate commands to the hardware peripheral because each hardware vendor uses custom electronic register protocols.

3. Programming Tools & Language Translators

Computers can only execute machine code (binary 0s and 1s). Human programmers write source code in high-level programming languages (Python, C++, Java) or low-level assembly language. Language translators bridge this gap.

A. Assembler

An Assembler translates low-level Assembly Language source code (which uses mnemonic codes like MOV, ADD, SUB) into machine language (binary 0s and 1s).

B. Compiler vs Interpreter

High-level languages require either a Compiler or an Interpreter to translate human-readable source code into machine code.

Feature Compiler Interpreter
Translation MethodTranslates the entire source code into machine code in one single attempt.Translates and executes source code line-by-line sequentially.
Intermediate FileGenerates a permanent standalone executable binary file (e.g., .exe or .o).Does not generate a standalone intermediate executable file.
Error ReportingLists all syntax errors together at the end of the full compilation process.Stops execution immediately at the very first line where an error occurs.
Execution SpeedFaster execution after compilation because target machine code is already built.Slower execution because translation happens dynamically during runtime.
Memory RequirementRequires more memory to store object code during compilation.Requires less memory during translation.
Example LanguagesC, C++, Rust, Go.Python, Ruby, JavaScript (JIT interpreted).

4. Application Software

Application software consists of programs designed to accomplish specific user-oriented tasks, workflows, or problem-solving operations.

A. General-Purpose Application Software

Off-the-shelf software developed for mass use across diverse fields. Users do not need customized programming.

  • Word Processors: Document creation, editing, formatting (e.g., MS Word, Google Docs, LibreOffice Writer).
  • Spreadsheets: Tabular data calculation, charting, statistical analysis (e.g., MS Excel, Google Sheets).
  • Database Management Systems (DBMS): Storing, querying, and managing structured data tables (e.g., MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle).
  • Presentation Software: Slide deck creation with multimedia animations (e.g., MS PowerPoint, Google Slides).
  • Web Browsers: Retrieving and rendering web pages (e.g., Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox).

B. Specific-Purpose / Customized Software

Tailor-made software designed and coded to meet the exact business requirements of a specific organization or enterprise.

  • School Management System: Handles student admissions, fee tracking, timetable generation, and report cards.
  • Hospital Information System: Manages patient records, doctor appointments, pharmacy stock, and medical billing.
  • Payroll Management System: Calculates employee salaries, tax deductions, provident fund, and generates payslips.
  • Airline / Railway Reservation System: Handles seat inventory, ticket booking, cancellation, and seat allocation.

Revision Questions & Answers

Q1: What is a device driver and why is it necessary?
Ans: A device driver is a system software program that acts as a translator between the OS and a specific hardware peripheral, enabling the OS to issue control commands understood by the device.

Q2: Compare Compiler and Interpreter on error reporting.
Ans: A compiler reports all syntax errors together after scanning the full program. An interpreter stops execution immediately at the first line containing an error.

Q3: Give two examples of customized application software.
Ans: 1. Railway Reservation System, 2. School Fee Management System.

subject: CS
title: Operating System Functions & Interfaces
description: Original study guide on Operating Systems for Class 11 CS. Explains OS definition, 5 primary functions (Process, Memory, File, Device, Security management), and User Interfaces (CLI vs GUI vs Touch).
content:
1. What is an Operating System?

An Operating System (OS) is the master system software program that acts as an interface between computer hardware and the human user or application software. It acts as an overall Resource Manager, controlling CPU execution time, memory allocation, storage files, and peripheral I/O access.

Why is an OS Necessary?

  • Hides Hardware Complexity: Users write high-level code or click buttons without managing individual electrical transistors or disk sectors.
  • Resource Abstraction: Provides standardized APIs for applications to request memory, open files, or print documents safely.
  • System Protection: Prevents unauthorized programs from overwriting system memory or accessing restricted hardware resources.

2. Major Functions of an Operating System

The OS performs five fundamental resource management functions:

A. Process Management

A process is a program in active execution. The OS manages process lifecycle, CPU scheduling, and process synchronization.

  • Allocates CPU time slices to active processes using scheduling algorithms (e.g., First-Come-First-Served, Round Robin, Priority Scheduling).
  • Creates, suspends, resumes, and terminates processes.
  • Handles multi-tasking so users can run multiple applications simultaneously.

B. Memory Management

Primary memory (RAM) is a limited shared resource. The OS controls allocation and tracking of memory blocks.

  • Keeps track of which parts of RAM are currently in use and by which process.
  • Dynamically allocates RAM when an application requests memory and deallocates it when the process closes.
  • Implements Virtual Memory (using disk space as swap memory) when active processes exceed physical RAM capacity.

C. File Management

The OS organizes stored data into logical structures called files and directories (folders).

  • Provides mechanisms for file creation, opening, reading, writing, renaming, and deletion.
  • Maintains file allocation tables (e.g., NTFS, FAT32, ext4) mapping logical files to physical disk sectors.
  • Enforces file access permissions (Read, Write, Execute) for security.

D. Device / I/O Management

Coordinates incoming and outgoing data signals between CPU and external hardware peripherals.

  • Uses specialized Device Drivers to communicate with hardware peripherals.
  • Implements Buffering: Temporary memory storage area used to compensate for speed differences between fast CPU and slower I/O devices.
  • Implements Spooling (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line): Queues data jobs sent to slow devices like printers so the CPU is freed immediately.

E. Security and User Interface Management

  • Authentication & Authorization: Verifies user identity via passwords, PINs, or biometrics and prevents unauthorized access to confidential files.
  • User Interface Provision: Displays shell environment (command prompt or graphical desktop) allowing users to interact with the computer.

3. Types of OS User Interfaces

The user interface (UI) is the visual or textual environment provided by the OS to accept commands from the user.

Interface Type Key Features Advantages Examples
Command Line Interface (CLI) User types text commands at a command prompt interface. Lightweight, consumes very little RAM, fast execution, scriptable. MS-DOS, Linux Bash Terminal, Command Prompt.
Graphical User Interface (GUI) Uses visual elements: Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointers (WIMP). Highly intuitive, beginner-friendly, visual drag-and-drop feedback. Windows 11, macOS, Ubuntu GNOME.
Touch / Natural User Interface (NUI) Responds to finger touch gestures, voice inputs, or facial tracking. No physical keyboard/mouse required, natural direct interaction. Android, iOS, iPadOS.

Revision Questions & Answers

Q1: Explain the difference between Buffering and Spooling in OS.
Ans: Buffering uses a temporary RAM buffer to smooth out speed differences during data transfer. Spooling queues print jobs or I/O data onto a disk file so the CPU can immediately resume other tasks.

Q2: What is Virtual Memory?
Ans: Virtual memory is a memory management technique where the OS uses a portion of secondary storage (swap space) to extend physical RAM when memory is exhausted.

Q3: State two advantages of CLI over GUI.
Ans: 1. Consumes much lower system RAM and CPU overhead, 2. Enables fast automation via command scripting.

title: Boolean Logic, Truth Tables & De Morgan's Laws
description: Original Class 11 CS study module on Boolean Logic. Covers Boolean variables, fundamental logic gates (NOT, AND, OR), derived gates (NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR), truth tables, logic circuits, and step-by-step De Morgan's Laws truth table proofs.
content:
1. Introduction to Boolean Algebra

Boolean Logic (developed by mathematician George Boole in 1854) is a branch of algebra that deals with binary variables that take only two logical truth values: True (1) or False (0).

Digital computer circuits operate on high voltage (represented as 1) and low voltage (represented as 0). Thus, Boolean logic forms the theoretical foundation for designing digital logic circuits inside CPUs.

2. Fundamental Logic Gates

A Logic Gate is an electronic circuit with one or more binary input signals that produces a single binary output signal based on a logical rule.

A. NOT Gate (Inverter)

Takes a single input and produces its logical complement (reverses 0 to 1, and 1 to 0).

Boolean Expression: Y = A' or Y = \bar{A} or Y = NOT A

Input AOutput Y
01
10

B. AND Gate

Produces an output of 1 if and only if ALL inputs are 1. Performs logical multiplication.

Boolean Expression: Y = A · B or Y = AB

ABOutput Y (A·B)
000
010
100
111

C. OR Gate

Produces an output of 1 if AT LEAST ONE input is 1. Performs logical addition.

Boolean Expression: Y = A + B

ABOutput Y (A+B)
000
011
101
111

3. Derived and Universal Logic Gates

A. NAND Gate (NOT + AND) - Universal Gate

Inverts the output of an AND gate. Output is 0 only when all inputs are 1. It is called a Universal Gate because any Boolean logic circuit can be built using only NAND gates.

Boolean Expression: Y = \overline{A · B}

B. NOR Gate (NOT + OR) - Universal Gate

Inverts the output of an OR gate. Output is 1 only when all inputs are 0. NOR is also a Universal Gate.

Boolean Expression: Y = \overline{A + B}

C. XOR Gate (Exclusive-OR)

Produces an output of 1 when the inputs are DIFFERENT (odd number of 1s).

Boolean Expression: Y = A \oplus B = A\bar{B} + \bar{A}B

D. XNOR Gate (Exclusive-NOR)

Inverts the XOR output. Produces an output of 1 when the inputs are SAME (even number of 1s).

Boolean Expression: Y = \overline{A \oplus B} = AB + \bar{A}\bar{B}

4. De Morgan's Laws & Truth Table Proofs

Augustus De Morgan proposed two fundamental theorems that relate AND, OR, and NOT operations. These laws are essential for simplifying complex digital circuits.

De Morgan's Laws Statements

First Law: The complement of a logical sum equals the product of individual complements.
Formula: \overline{A + B} = \bar{A} · \bar{B}

Second Law: The complement of a logical product equals the sum of individual complements.
Formula: \overline{A · B} = \bar{A} + \bar{B}

Verification of De Morgan's First Law using Truth Table:

To prove \overline{A + B} = \bar{A} · \bar{B}, compare Column 5 and Column 8:

A B A + B LHS: \overline{A + B} \bar{A} \bar{B} RHS: \bar{A} · \bar{B}
0001111
0110100
1010010
1110000

Since LHS column (\overline{A + B}) is identical to RHS column (\bar{A} · \bar{B}) for all input combinations, De Morgan's First Law is proved!

Verification of De Morgan's Second Law using Truth Table:

To prove \overline{A · B} = \bar{A} + \bar{B}, compare LHS and RHS columns:

A B A · B LHS: \overline{A · B} \bar{A} \bar{B} RHS: \bar{A} + \bar{B}
0001111
0101101
1001011
1110000

Since LHS column (\overline{A · B}) is identical to RHS column (\bar{A} + \bar{B}) for all input combinations, De Morgan's Second Law is proved!

5. Essential Laws of Boolean Algebra

  • Identity Law: A + 0 = A, A · 1 = A
  • Null / Dominance Law: A + 1 = 1, A · 0 = 0
  • Idempotent Law: A + A = A, A · A = A
  • Involution / Double Complement Law: \overline{\bar{A}} = A
  • Complementarity Law: A + \bar{A} = 1, A · \bar{A} = 0
  • Commutative Law: A + B = B + A, A · B = B · A
  • Associative Law: (A + B) + C = A + (B + C), (A · B) · C = A · (B · C)
  • Distributive Law: A · (B + C) = AB + AC, A + (B · C) = (A + B) · (A + C)
  • Absorption Law: A + AB = A, A · (A + B) = A

Revision Questions & Answers

Q1: Why are NAND and NOR called Universal Gates?
Ans: Because any fundamental logic gate (NOT, AND, OR) or complex digital logic circuit can be constructed using only NAND gates or only NOR gates.

Q2: State De Morgan's Second Law.
Ans: The complement of a logical product of variables is equal to the sum of their individual complements: \overline{A · B} = \bar{A} + \bar{B}.

Q3: What is the output of an XOR gate when both inputs are 1?
Ans: Output is 0 (False), because XOR produces 1 only when inputs are different.

title: Number Systems & Conversion Techniques
description: Original Class 11 CS study module on Number Systems. Features Binary, Octal, Decimal, and Hexadecimal base explanations and step-by-step worked conversion algorithms.
content:
1. What is a Number System?

A Number System is a mathematical framework for representing quantities using symbols called digits. The total number of unique digits available in a number system is called its Base or Radix.

The Four Positional Number Systems

Number System Base (r) Valid Digits / Symbols Example Value
Decimal100, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9$(254)_{10}$
Binary20, 1$(11111110)_2$
Octal80, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7$(376)_8$
Hexadecimal160-9, A(10), B(11), C(12), D(13), E(14), F(15)$(FE)_{16}$

2. Step-by-Step Conversion Algorithms with Solved Examples

Method 1: Decimal to Any Base (Binary / Octal / Hexadecimal)

Algorithm: Successive division of the decimal integer by the target base ($r$). Record the remainder at each step until quotient becomes 0. Read remainders from bottom to top (Most Significant Bit to Least Significant Bit).

Example 1.1: Convert $(25)_{10}$ to Binary

  • $25 \div 2 = 12$, Remainder = 1 (LSB)
  • $12 \div 2 = 6$, Remainder = 0
  • $6 \div 2 = 3$, Remainder = 0
  • $3 \div 2 = 1$, Remainder = 1
  • $1 \div 2 = 0$, Remainder = 1 (MSB)

Reading remainders bottom-to-top gives: $(25)_{10} = (11001)_2$

Example 1.2: Convert $(175)_{10}$ to Octal

  • $175 \div 8 = 21$, Remainder = 7 (LSB)
  • $21 \div 8 = 2$, Remainder = 5
  • $2 \div 8 = 0$, Remainder = 2 (MSB)

Reading remainders bottom-to-top gives: $(175)_{10} = (257)_8$

Example 1.3: Convert $(458)_{10}$ to Hexadecimal

  • $458 \div 16 = 28$, Remainder = 10 (which is hex A)
  • $28 \div 16 = 1$, Remainder = 12 (which is hex C)
  • $1 \div 16 = 0$, Remainder = 1 (MSB)

Reading remainders bottom-to-top gives: $(458)_{10} = (1CA)_{16}$

Method 2: Any Base to Decimal (Binary / Octal / Hexadecimal to Decimal)

Algorithm: Multiply each digit by positional weight $Base^{\text{position}}$ (where position starts at 0 from rightmost digit LSB) and sum up all terms.

Example 2.1: Convert $(110101)_2$ to Decimal

$= (1 \times 2^5) + (1 \times 2^4) + (0 \times 2^3) + (1 \times 2^2) + (0 \times 2^1) + (1 \times 2^0)$
$= 32 + 16 + 0 + 4 + 0 + 1 = (53)_{10}$

Example 2.2: Convert $(3A7)_{16}$ to Decimal

Note: $A = 10$
$= (3 \times 16^2) + (10 \times 16^1) + (7 \times 16^0)$
$= (3 \times 256) + (10 \times 16) + (7 \times 1) = 768 + 160 + 7 = (935)_{10}$

Method 3: Direct Grouping Conversions (Binary <--> Octal & Hexadecimal)

A. Binary to Octal (3-bit Grouping)

Group binary digits into sets of 3 from right to left (pad with leading 0s if necessary). Replace each 3-bit group with its single octal digit.

Convert $(1101011)_2$ to Octal:
Grouping from right: 001 | 101 | 011
Values: 1 | 5 | 3 → $(153)_8$

B. Binary to Hexadecimal (4-bit Grouping)

Group binary digits into sets of 4 from right to left. Replace each 4-bit group with its single hex digit (0-9, A-F).

Convert $(110101101)_2$ to Hexadecimal:
Grouping from right: 0001 | 1010 | 1101
Values: 1 | A | D → $(1AD)_{16}$

C. Hexadecimal to Octal (via Binary intermediate)

Convert $(2F)_16$ to Octal:
1. Expand Hex to 4-bit Binary: $2 ightarrow 0010$, $F ightarrow 1111$ → $(00101111)_2$
2. Regroup into 3-bit Octal groups from right: 000 | 101 | 111
3. Values: 0 | 5 | 7 → $(57)_8$

Revision Questions & Answers

Q1: Convert $(10110)_2$ to Decimal.
Ans: $(1 \times 2^4) + (0 \times 2^3) + (1 \times 2^2) + (1 \times 2^1) + (0 \times 2^0) = 16 + 0 + 4 + 2 + 0 = (22)_{10}$.

Q2: What is the binary equivalent of Hexadecimal digit 'B'?
Ans: Hex 'B' represents decimal 11. In 4-bit binary, $(11)_{10} = (1011)_2$.

Q3: Convert $(74)_8$ to Binary.
Ans: Expand each digit to 3 bits: $7 ightarrow 111$, $4 ightarrow 100$. Result = $(111100)_2$.

subject: CS
title: Character Encoding Schemes: ASCII, ISCII & Unicode
description: Original Class 11 CS study module on Encoding Schemes. Explains why encoding is needed, ASCII 7-bit/8-bit ranges, ISCII Indian language script standards, and Unicode (UTF-8, UTF-32).
content:
1. Why Do We Need Character Encoding Schemes?

Digital computers process and store everything as binary sequences of 0s and 1s. However, humans communicate using natural languages comprising alphabets (A-Z, a-z), numbers (0-9), punctuation marks, and special symbols.

An Encoding Scheme is a standardized lookup rule that maps every human character to a unique numeric binary code. When a key is pressed on a keyboard, the hardware generates a numeric binary code, which the computer translates into text using an encoding standard.

2. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange)

Developed in the 1960s by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI), ASCII is the most widely adopted foundational character encoding standard for English text.

A. 7-bit ASCII

  • Uses 7 bits to represent each character.
  • Can encode $2^7 = 128$ unique characters (decimal code values 0 to 127).
  • Codes 0-31 and 127 represent non-printable control characters (e.g., Line Feed, Carriage Return, Backspace, Tab).
  • Codes 32-126 represent printable characters (letters, numbers, space, punctuation).

B. 8-bit Extended ASCII

  • Uses 8 bits (1 Byte) to represent characters.
  • Can encode $2^8 = 256$ unique characters (decimal code values 0 to 255).
  • The first 128 codes (0-127) are identical to standard 7-bit ASCII. Codes 128-255 encode additional foreign symbols, accented characters, and graphic line characters.

Important ASCII Code Ranges (Must Memorize for Class 11 Exams)

  • Uppercase Letters ('A' to 'Z'): Decimal 65 to 90 (Binary: 01000001 to 01011010)
  • Lowercase Letters ('a' to 'z'): Decimal 97 to 122 (Binary: 01100001 to 01111010)
  • Numeric Digits ('0' to '9'): Decimal 48 to 57 (Binary: 00110000 to 00111001)
  • Space Character (' '): Decimal 32 (Binary: 00100000)

Notice: Lowercase ASCII code = Uppercase ASCII code + 32! (e.g., 'A'=65, 'a'=65+32=97).

3. ISCII (Indian Script Code for Information Interchange)

Developed in the late 1980s by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and C-DAC, ISCII is an 8-bit encoding standard designed specifically for Indian languages.

Key Features of ISCII

  • Encodes text for 10 major Indian scripts: Devanagari, Punjabi (Gurmukhi), Gujarati, Oriya, Bengali, Assamese, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, and Tamil.
  • Bilingual Compatibility: Retains standard 7-bit ASCII in the lower half (code 0-127). The upper half (codes 128-255) contains characters for Indian scripts.
  • Uses a common phonetic matrix layout across Indian languages, making translation between Indian scripts straightforward.

4. Unicode Standard

While ASCII is limited to English and ISCII is limited to Indian scripts, modern computing requires a universal encoding system that can represent every written language worldwide (Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, Cyrillic, mathematical symbols, emojis).

Unicode is a global encoding standard maintained by the Unicode Consortium that assigns a unique numeric Code Point (written as U+XXXX) to every character regardless of platform, language, or device.

Major Unicode Encoding Formats

A. UTF-8 (Unicode Transformation Format - 8-bit)

  • Variable-length encoding: Uses between 1 to 4 bytes (8 to 32 bits) per character depending on the symbol.
  • 100% ASCII Compatible: Standard ASCII characters (0-127) are encoded using exactly 1 byte, making UTF-8 file sizes compact for English text.
  • Web Dominance: Over 98% of all websites worldwide use UTF-8 as their primary encoding standard.

B. UTF-32 (Unicode Transformation Format - 32-bit)

  • Fixed-length encoding: Uses exactly 4 bytes (32 bits) for every single character.
  • Simple Indexing: Every character occupies fixed width in memory, simplifying string indexing in software code.
  • Disadvantage: High memory usage (4 times more RAM/disk space than ASCII for basic English text).

Summary Comparison of Encoding Schemes

Encoding Bit Length Total Unique Characters Primary Usage
7-bit ASCII7 bits128Basic English text
8-bit ASCII8 bits (1 byte)256English + Western symbols
ISCII8 bits (1 byte)256Indian language scripts
UTF-8Variable (1 to 4 bytes)1,114,112 code pointsGlobal Web & modern OS
UTF-32Fixed (4 bytes)1,114,112 code pointsInternal string processing

Revision Questions & Answers

Q1: What is the decimal ASCII value of character 'K'?
Ans: Since 'A'=65, 'K' is the 11th letter of alphabet. Code = $65 + (11 - 1) = 65 + 10 = \mathbf{75}$.

Q2: Why is UTF-8 widely preferred over UTF-32 for web applications?
Ans: Because UTF-8 uses variable length (1 byte for ASCII), conserving bandwidth and memory while maintaining backwards compatibility with ASCII.

Q3: What does ISCII stand for?
Ans: Indian Script Code for Information Interchange.

description: Master styles, image formatting, text wrapping, drawing objects, templates, automated tables of contents, and mail merge wizard in LibreOffice Writer.
content:
1. Understanding Styles in Word Processing

A style is a set of formats that you can apply to selected pages, text, frames, and other elements in your document to quickly change their appearance. Instead of applying individual formatting attributes one by one, a single style applies a unified set of formats simultaneously.

Advantages of Styles:

  • Ensures consistent formatting throughout multi-page documents.
  • Significantly reduces manual formatting effort and saves time.
  • Allows instant global updates across the entire document when modified.
  • Crucial for generating an automated Table of Contents (TOC).

2. Categories of Styles in LibreOffice Writer

  • Paragraph Style: Controls all aspects of paragraph layout including text alignment, line spacing, margins, indentation, and borders.
  • Character Style: Modifies selected words or characters within a paragraph (font family, font size, bold, italics, font color) without affecting overall paragraph layout.
  • Page Style: Defines page layout, page size, margins, headers, footers, borders, page numbering, and background color.
  • Frame Style: Controls formatting of graphic boxes, frames, and captions.
  • List Style: Configures numbering schemes, bullets, and indentation levels for ordered and unordered lists.

3. Working with Images & Objects

Images support textual content and improve visual communication in formal documentation:

  • Inserting: Insert > Image..., drag-and-drop from file manager, or copy-paste from clipboard.
  • Resizing: Always use corner handles to preserve aspect ratio and avoid distorting image proportions.
  • Cropping: Eliminates unwanted outer areas. Writer supports 'Keep scale' and 'Keep image size' modes.
  • Anchoring: Locks the image reference point: To Page, To Paragraph, To Character, or As Character.
  • Text Wrapping: Determines how text flows around objects: None, Parallel (Wrap Around), Optimal, or Through.
  • Grouping: Shift-click multiple drawing shapes -> Right-click -> Group -> Group to treat them as a single movable object.

4. Templates & Table of Contents

Templates: A template is a pre-designed sample document serving as the foundation for creating new documents with pre-defined styles, page settings, logos, and layouts (File > Templates > Save As Template).

Table of Contents (TOC): Automated navigational hierarchy listing document headings and page numbers. Headings must use standard Heading 1, 2, 3 styles. Insert via Insert > Table of Contents and Index. Always check 'Protected against manual changes' and click 'Update Index' when document pages shift.

5. Mail Merge Automation

Mail Merge is used to produce multiple personalized documents (letters, certificates, notices, labels) from one standard master document and a structured data source:

  • Main Document: The master text that remains common across all copies.
  • Data Source: A spreadsheet, database, or text table containing variable records (Names, Addresses, Marks).
  • Merge Fields: Placeholders (e.g., <Name>, <Address>) inserted where individual data will appear.
  • Merged Output: The personalized generated output ready for printing or email distribution.

title: Electronic Spreadsheets (Advanced)
description: Comprehensive notes covering Data Consolidation, Subtotals, What-If Scenarios, Goal Seek, Solver, Linking Sheets, Hyperlinks, Sharing, Track Changes, and Macros in LibreOffice Calc.
content:
1. Data Consolidation

Data Consolidation (Data > Consolidate...) merges data from multiple independent worksheets or workbooks into a single master summary sheet. Available statistical functions include SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MAX, MIN, and PRODUCT.

Options: Select Row labels and Column labels to match data headers automatically even if rows appear in different orders across source sheets. Enable Link to source data to ensure summary tables update when source cells change.

2. Subtotals and What-If Scenarios

  • Subtotals (Data > Subtotals...): Automatically groups related rows and calculates category-wise subtotals and grand totals. Crucial Rule: Data MUST be sorted by the grouping column before applying Subtotals.
  • What-If Scenarios (Tools > Scenarios...): Saved sets of cell input values used to model hypothetical outcomes on the same worksheet without creating multiple duplicate sheets (e.g., Best-Case, Realistic, Worst-Case budget forecasts).

3. Goal Seek and Solver

  • Goal Seek (Tools > Goal Seek...): Reverse calculation tool that determines the input value needed in a designated cell to achieve a specific target formula result. Works with one changing cell.
  • Solver (Tools > Solver...): Advanced optimization tool that handles multiple changing variable cells subjected to defined limiting constraints (e.g., maximum budget caps, non-negative integer limits).

4. Linking Spreadsheets and Hyperlinks

  • Multi-Sheet Referencing: Calc uses =SheetName.CellAddress (e.g., =Term1.B4). Excel uses =SheetName!CellAddress.
  • Hyperlinks: Insert via Ctrl + K. Absolute Hyperlink stores complete path (breaks only if target moves). Relative Hyperlink stores path relative to current folder (works across transferred folders).

5. Sharing, Reviewing, and Macros

  • Sharing (Tools > Share Spreadsheet...): Enables concurrent multi-user editing across local networks.
  • Record Changes (Edit > Track Changes > Record): Highlights modified cells with colored borders and author tooltips. Review via Accept or Reject dialogs.
  • Macros: Recorded sequences of commands and keystrokes saved to automate repetitive tasks (Tools > Macros > Record Macro). Can be assigned to shortcut keys or buttons.

title: Database Management System (DBMS & SQL)
description: Master RDBMS fundamentals, Tables, Tuples, Attributes, Keys (Primary, Candidate, Alternate, Foreign), Data Types, Design View, Referential Integrity, Relationships, and SQL DDL/DML.
content:
1. Database Concepts & RDBMS Terminology

A Database is an organized collection of logically related data stored electronically. A DBMS acts as the interface to define, update, query, and manage data while controlling redundancy and inconsistency.

  • Relation (Table): Two-dimensional table with columns and rows.
  • Tuple (Record / Row): Horizontal row representing a complete entity record.
  • Attribute (Field / Column): Vertical column representing a specific property.
  • Degree: Total number of columns (attributes) in a table.
  • Cardinality: Total number of rows (tuples) in a table.

2. Keys in Database

KeyDefinition
Primary Key (PK)Uniquely identifies each tuple in a relation. Cannot accept duplicate values and CANNOT BE NULL.
Candidate KeyAny attribute capable of uniquely identifying tuples in a relation.
Alternate KeyCandidate keys not selected as the primary key.
Foreign Key (FK)Field in a child table matching the Primary Key of a parent table, linking the two tables.

3. Referential Integrity & Table Relationships

Referential Integrity ensures that foreign key values in a child table always match an existing primary key in the parent table, preventing orphaned records. Cascade rules include Restrict (No Action), Cascade Update, Cascade Delete, and Set NULL.

Relationships are established in the Tools > Relationships... window: One-to-One (1:1), One-to-Many (1:N), and Many-to-Many (M:N).

4. Structured Query Language (SQL)

  • DDL (Data Definition Language): Defines schemas (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE).
  • DML (Data Manipulation Language): Manipulates records (SELECT, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE).
  • WHERE Filtering: =, <>, >, <, AND, OR, BETWEEN ... AND, IN, LIKE ('A%'), IS NULL.
  • Sorting & Aggregates: ORDER BY col DESC, COUNT(*), SUM(), AVG(), MAX(), MIN().

5. Forms and Reports

  • Form: Interactive graphical interface for intuitive record entry, viewing, and modification one by one.
  • Report: Formatted, printable summary document generated from tables or queries for executive review and printing.

title: Web Applications and Security
description: Comprehensive notes covering Computer Accessibility Options, Networking Architectures, Instant Messaging, Blogs, Online Transactions, Cyber Security Threats, Antivirus, Ergonomics, and Workplace Safety.
content:
1. Computer Accessibility Options

Accessibility features in Windows (Control Panel > Ease of Access) assist users with physical, sensory, or cognitive impairments:

  • StickyKeys: Keeps modifier keys (Shift, Ctrl, Alt, Win) active sequentially so users press one key at a time. Press Shift 5 times.
  • FilterKeys: Ignores rapid, repeated keystrokes caused by hand tremors. Hold right Shift for 8 seconds.
  • ToggleKeys: Plays high/low audio beeps when locking keys (Caps Lock, Num Lock, Scroll Lock) are toggled.
  • SoundSentry & ShowSounds: Provide visual warnings and captions for hearing-impaired users.
  • High Contrast: Inverts screen colors to high-contrast palettes for enhanced visual readability.
  • MouseKeys & SerialKeys: Controls cursor with numeric keypad or serial assistive switches.

2. Networking Fundamentals

  • Network Types: PAN (<= 10m, Bluetooth), LAN (local building/campus), MAN (citywide, <= 50 km), WAN (global, Internet).
  • Network Architectures: Peer-to-Peer (P2P, equal peers, no central server) vs. Client-Server (centralized servers manage resources and security).
  • Hardware: NIC (MAC address), Modem (Modulation/Demodulation), Hub (broadcasts to all), Switch (intelligent directed routing), Router (packet routing across IP networks).
  • Internet Terms: WWW, URL, IP Address, DNS, ISP, Bandwidth.

3. Online Transactions & Cyber Security

  • Safe Online Transactions: Verify HTTPS and closed padlock icon, never share OTP/PIN/CVV, avoid public Wi-Fi for banking, enable Two-Factor Authentication (2FA).
  • Malware Threats: Virus (attaches to host files), Worm (self-replicating over networks), Trojan Horse (disguised as useful tool), Spyware & Keylogger (steals credentials), Ransomware (encrypts files for ransom).
  • Attacks: Phishing (fake emails/sites stealing credentials), Spoofing (forging identity), DoS/DDoS (flooding servers with fake traffic).
  • Defenses: Strong passwords (8-12 chars), Antivirus, Firewalls, regular OS updates, backups.

4. Workplace Health, Ergonomics & Safety

  • Ergonomics: Follow the 20-20-20 rule for eye strain (CVS), use lumbar-supported chairs, keep monitor at eye level, maintain flat wrists to prevent RSI.
  • Physical Safety: Keep computer cables inside conduits along walls to prevent trips and falls; clean liquid spills immediately.
  • Fire Safety & PASS: Use CO2 or dry powder on electrical fires (NEVER water). PASS technique: Pull pin, Aim at base of fire, Squeeze handle, Sweep side to side.
  • Evacuation: Sound alarm, use stairs (never elevators), gather at external Assembly Point.
